patches.old: \item \emph{Their product divides $\binom{2n}{n}$.} Each such prime appears in the factorization of $\binom{2n}{n}$ (by uniqueness), and they are distinct, so their product $\prod_{n<p\le2n}p$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$, and therefore $\prod_{n<p\le2n}p\le\binom{2n}{n}$.
patches.new: \item \emph{Their product divides $\binom{2n}{n}$.} Write the canonical factorization $\binom{2n}{n}=r_1^{b_1}\cdots r_j^{b_j}$ (\cref{eq:primes-fta}). If a prime $p$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$, then by the repeated Euclid's lemma $p$ divides some $r_i$, so $p=r_i$: every such $p$ is one of the $r_i$, with exponent $b_i\ge1$. The primes in $(n,2n]$ are distinct, so they are distinct members of the list $r_1,\dots,r_j$. Hence $\binom{2n}{n}=\bigl(\prod_{n<p\le2n}p\bigr)\cdot c$, where $c$ is the product of all remaining prime factors (each $r_i$ taken $b_i-1$ more times if it is one of our primes, $b_i$ times otherwise), a positive integer. So $\prod_{n<p\le2n}p$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$, and therefore $\prod_{n<p\le2n}p\le\binom{2n}{n}$.

patches.old: \textbf{A warning about numerical evidence.} In every case ever computed directly, $\pi(x)<\mathrm{Li}(x)$. Yet Littlewood proved in 1914 that $\pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x)$ changes sign infinitely often. The first sign change is known to occur only at astronomically large $x$. Tables, however large, can mislead.
patches.new: \textbf{A warning about numerical evidence.} In every case computed directly (including all of \cref{tab:primes-pi}), $\pi(x)<\mathrm{Li}(x)$. Yet Littlewood proved in 1914 that $\pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x)$ changes sign infinitely often. No sign change has been found by direct computation; the literature proves that the first one lies below an explicit but astronomically large bound, far beyond any table. Tables, however large, can mislead.
